title: Battle of Cannae
description: Largest battle of the Second Punic War (216 BC)
wiki_lead:
The Battle of Cannae (; Latin: [ˈkanːae̯]) was a key engagement of the Second Punic War between the Roman Republic and Carthage, fought on 2 August 216 BC near the ancient village of Cannae in Apulia, southeast Italy. The Carthaginians and their allies, led by Hannibal, surrounded and practically annihilated a larger Roman and Italian army under the consuls Lucius Aemilius Paullus and Gaius Terentius Varro. It is regarded as one of the greatest tactical feats in military history and one of the worst defeats in Roman history, and it cemented Hannibal's reputation as one of antiquity's greatest tacticians.
Having recovered from their losses at Trebia (218 BC) and Lake Trasimene (217 BC), the Romans decided to engage Hannibal at Cannae, with approximately 86,000 Roman and allied socii troops. They massed their heavy infantry in a deeper formation than usual, while Hannibal used the double envelopment tactic and surrounded his enemy, trapping the majority of the Roman army, who were then slaughtered. Later historians and military strategists have used Cannae as an exemplary battle of annihilation. The loss of life on the Roman side meant it was one of the most lethal single days of fighting in history; historian Adrian Goldsworthy equates the death toll at Cannae to "the massed slaughter of the British Army on the first day of the Somme offensive in 1916". Only about 15,000 Romans, most of whom were from the garrisons of the camps and had not taken part in the battle, survived. Following the defeat, Capua and several other Italian city-states defected from the Roman Republic to Carthage.
As news of this defeat reached Rome, the city was gripped in panic. Authorities resorted to extraordinary measures, which included consulting the Sibylline Books, dispatching a delegation led by Quintus Fabius Pictor to consult the Delphic oracle in Greece, and burying four people alive as a sacrifice to their gods. To raise two new legions, the authorities lowered the draft age and enlisted criminals, debtors and even slaves. Despite the extreme loss of men and equipment, and a second massive defeat later that same year at Silva Litana, the Romans refused to surrender to Hannibal. His offer to ransom survivors was brusquely refused. The Romans fought for 14 more years until they achieved victory at the Battle of Zama.

Strategic background

Shortly after the start of the Second Punic War, Hannibal crossed into Italy by traversing the Pyrenees and the Alps during the summer and early autumn of 218 BC. He quickly won major victories over the Romans at Trebia and at Lake Trasimene. After these losses, the Romans appointed Quintus Fabius Maximus Verrucosus as dictator to deal with the threat.

grok_lead: The Battle of Cannae was a decisive engagement of the Second Punic War, fought on August 2, 216 BC, near the village of Cannae in Apulia, southeastern Italy, where Carthaginian general Hannibal Barca annihilated a much larger Roman army through masterful envelopment tactics. The battle occurred during the third year of Hannibal 's invasion of Italy, following his earlier victories at the Trebia (218 BC) and Lake Trasimene (217 BC), which had already strained Roman resources and morale. Rome, determined to crush the Carthaginian threat, assembled its largest army to date under the joint command of consuls Lucius Aemilius Paullus and Gaius Terentius Varro, who alternated daily command; Paullus favored caution, while Varro pushed for aggressive action. Hannibal, commanding a multinational force of approximately 40,000 infantry (including Iberian, Celtic, and African troops) and 10,000 cavalry, positioned his army along the Aufidus River to exploit the flat terrain near Cannae. The Romans fielded about 80,000 legionaries and allies in heavy infantry, supported by 6,000 cavalry, deploying in a deep, dense formation intended to overwhelm the enemy center. As the battle unfolded, Hannibal deliberately weakened his center with less reliable Celtic and Spanish infantry in a crescent-shaped line, baiting the Romans into a frontal assault while his elite African infantry held the flanks and his superior Numidian and Iberian cavalry dominated the wings. Under Varro's command on the fateful day, the Romans advanced and shattered the Carthaginian center, pushing deep into the formation; this created an opportunity for Hannibal's cavalry to rout the Roman horse on both flanks, then wheel inward to attack the Roman rear. The African infantry then pivoted to close the encirclement, trapping the Roman legions in a deadly " cauldron " where they were systematically slaughtered in close quarters, unable to maneuver or retreat effectively. The outcome was catastrophic for Rome, with ancient accounts reporting around 70,000 Roman soldiers killedâincluding one consul ( Lucius Aemilius Paullus) and numerous senatorsâand about 10,000 captured, while only roughly 3,000 escaped; Carthaginian losses were minimal, with Polybius reporting approximately 5,700 (mostly from the center troops) and Livy reporting 8,000. Despite the annihilation of two Roman consular armies, Hannibal refrained from marching on Rome itself, instead seeking to consolidate alliances in southern Italy and encourage Roman defection. The battle's tactical brilliance, particularly the double envelopment, has since been studied as a paradigm of annihilation warfare and one of the most significant defeats in Roman military history, influencing strategies from antiquity to modern times.
